prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates nearby body parts and furniture from the dark, more distant background: an arm enters from the upper right in frame 1, remains about 0.3–0.8 m away across frames 2–3, and a bent leg becomes the nearest region, roughly 0.2–0.5 m away, in frame 4. A broad seat or chair surface lies in front of the wearer at approximately 0.5–1.5 m in frames 1–3, while another pale chair-like object occupies the right side of frame 5 at roughly 0.5–1 m; the background is probably beyond 2 m. Across the strip, the nearby arm shifts leftward and partly out of view, the leg moves prominently into the right-front field, and the final chair appears as the camera turns right. These depth relationships are harder to judge from the dark RGB frames, but the smooth gradients, clipped bright limbs, missing boundaries, and monocular scale ambiguity make the metre estimates and fine separations unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates large foreground regions in frames 2–4, including a person-shaped arm/body region extending diagonally across the view and a large near region corresponding to the bent leg in frame 4; it also outlines a broad seat or furniture surface beneath or behind the arm. It makes occlusion clearer: the arm overlaps the furniture in frames 2–3, parts of the person continue beyond the top or right image boundaries, and the close leg blocks much of the background in frame 4. The changing masks support a leftward sweep of the arm followed by the leg entering the right-front view, but almost nothing is segmented in frames 1 and 5 despite visible scene structure. Labels such as “banana” and “cup” do not match the RGB evidence, adjacent masks merge or split inconsistently, and the map cannot provide dependable metric distances or facing and gaze direction.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only a small magenta hand skeleton near the upper-central area of frame 3, placing that hand above and slightly right of the corresponding nearby arm, roughly 0.5–1 m from the camera wearer and plausibly within the wearer’s arm reach. The hand’s keypoints suggest its orientation in the image plane, but they do not reliably establish palm direction, the person’s facing direction, gaze, or whether the hand is in front of or behind another body part. No body skeleton appears, and the prominent arms and leg visible in the RGB are missed across the other frames, so approach, retreat, turning, inter-person spacing, and reach for anyone else cannot be tracked. The isolated hand localization is difficult to extract from the dark RGB alone, but its tiny, crowded keypoints and the extensive missed detections make this pose map highly unreliable.
